lead: At microwave frequencies a component is not tested with a multimeter. Power enters and leaves through ports, and each port is a transmission-line cross-section with a fixed reference impedance Z₀, usually 50 Ω. The scattering matrix S collects the ratios of the waves leaving the ports to the waves arriving at them. It describes amplifiers, filters, couplers and antennas from about 1 GHz to 100 GHz, and every later chapter describes its component by its S-matrix.
prereq: You need: reflection coefficient Γ, VSWR and return loss on a transmission line (see Reflection coefficient, standing waves and VSWR), and complex numbers in polar form.

sections.h3: Waves in and out of a port

blocks.text: Z, Y, h and ABCD parameters need open-circuit or short-circuit tests. Above about 1 GHz an open end radiates, a short has inductance, and a transistor may oscillate when its port is shorted. A matched load is easy to build, so a microwave device is described by travelling waves at matched ports.
At port i, let aᵢ be the wave travelling into the device and bᵢ the wave travelling out. With RMS values, as used here, |aᵢ|² is the power arriving and |bᵢ|² the power leaving, in watts.

blocks.where: Vᵢ and Iᵢ are the total voltage and current at port i, Z₀ is the real reference impedance, aᵢ the incident wave and bᵢ the outgoing wave, both in √W.

blocks.text: For N ports the outgoing waves are linear combinations of the incoming ones: b = S a, where a and b are column vectors of length N and S is an N × N matrix. Each element is
Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ / aⱼ   with aₖ = 0 for every k ≠ j
blocks.where: every port except j ends in a matched load, so no wave enters it. Sᵢⱼ is a complex number: |Sᵢⱼ| is the amplitude ratio and its angle is the phase shift from port j to port i.

blocks.text: The array S is called the scattering matrix (S-matrix). Some syllabi write it as [S] and the waves as [b] = [S][a].

sections.h3: The four S-parameters of a two-port

blocks.text: Match port 2 (a₂ = 0) and drive port 1. Then b₁ = S₁₁a₁ and b₂ = S₂₁a₁. Match port 1 (a₁ = 0) and drive port 2: b₁ = S₁₂a₂ and b₂ = S₂₂a₂.

items: S₁₁: input reflection coefficient, port 2 matched.
S₂₁: forward transmission coefficient (forward voltage gain), port 2 matched.
S₁₂: reverse transmission coefficient, port 1 matched.
S₂₂: output reflection coefficient, port 1 matched.

blocks.text: Each magnitude is quoted in dB as a power ratio, so 20 log of the wave ratio.

head: Quantity
Formula
What the number tells you
rows: how far the reflected power is below the incident power
how far the power delivered to a matched load is below the incident power
standing-wave ratio at port 1 with port 2 matched
how far reverse transmission is below the incident power

blocks.text: When port 2 is not matched but ends in a load with reflection coefficient Γ<sub>L</sub>, the input reflection is no longer S₁₁:

blocks.where: the second term is the wave that crosses to port 2, reflects from the load and comes back. With Γ<sub>L</sub> = 0 it vanishes and Γin = S₁₁.

blocks.text: Three tests catch most errors in an exam answer. Apply all three to every matrix you write.

items: Reciprocal (no ferrite, no active device, no plasma): S = Sᵀ, so Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ. The matrix is symmetric.

Lossless: S†S = I, where S† is the conjugate transpose and I the identity. Each column has Σᵢ|Sᵢⱼ|² = 1 (all the power sent in at port j comes out somewhere), and any two different columns are orthogonal: Σᵢ Sᵢⱼ S*ᵢₖ = 0. A matrix with S†S = I is called unitary.
Matched at port i: Sᵢᵢ = 0. A fully matched device has a zero diagonal.

blocks.text: For a lossy device the column sums are less than 1, and 1 − Σᵢ|Sᵢⱼ|² is the fraction of the power entering port j that turns into heat.

The reference plane matters. Moving the reference plane of port n outward by a length l of matched line adds a phase θₙ = βl, where β = 2π/λg is the phase constant and λg the guide wavelength. A term Sᵢⱼ picks up e<sup>−j(θᵢ + θⱼ)</sup>: an off-diagonal term touching the moved port once gets e<sup>−jθ</sup>, and the diagonal term Sₙₙ, whose wave crosses the extra line twice, gets e<sup>−j2θ</sup>. Magnitudes do not change. S-parameters also depend on frequency and on Z₀, so quote both with every matrix.

examples.question: A 50 Ω two-port at 10 GHz has S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, S₂₁ = 0.9∠−30°, S₁₂ = 0 and S₂₂ = 0.1∠0°. Find (a) the return loss at port 1, (b) the insertion loss, (c) the input VSWR with port 2 matched and (d) the reverse isolation. Is the device reciprocal?
steps: Port 2 is matched, so a₂ = 0 and Γin = S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°; |S₁₁| = 0.2.
Insertion loss: IL = −20 log₁₀(0.9) = −20 × (−0.04576) = 0.92 dB. The phase −30° is a delay and does not change the loss.
S₁₂ = 0, so reverse isolation = −20 log₁₀(0) → ∞ dB: no wave travels from port 2 to port 1.
Reciprocity test: S₁₂ = 0 but S₂₁ = 0.9∠−30°, so S ≠ Sᵀ. The device is not reciprocal; it is unilateral, like an ideal buffer amplifier or an isolator.
examples.answer: RL = 13.98 dB, IL = 0.92 dB, input VSWR = 1.5, reverse isolation infinite; the device is not reciprocal.

examples.question: A 50 Ω two-port has S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, S₁₂ = S₂₁ = 0.8∠−60° and S₂₂ = 0.3∠0°. (a) Is it reciprocal? Is it lossless? (b) What fraction of the power entering port 1 is lost as heat when port 2 is matched? (c) Find Γin and the return loss at port 1 when port 2 is short-circuited. (d) Find the new S₁₁ and S₂₁ if the port-1 reference plane is moved outward by βl = 45°.
steps: Reciprocal: S₁₂ = S₂₁ = 0.8∠−60°, so S = Sᵀ. Yes.
Lossless test on column 1: |S₁₁|² + |S₂₁|² = 0.04 + 0.64 = 0.68 ≠ 1. Column 2: 0.64 + 0.09 = 0.73. The matrix is not unitary, so the device is lossy.
Heat with port 2 matched: 1 − 0.68 = 0.32, so 32 % of the power entering port 1 is absorbed; 4 % reflects and 64 % reaches the load.
Return loss = −20 log₁₀(0.617) = 4.19 dB: the wave reflected by the short comes back through the device.
Port-1 plane moved out by θ = 45°: S₁₁′ = 0.2∠−90° (twice θ); S₂₁′ = 0.8∠−105° (once); S₂₂ unchanged.
examples.answer: Reciprocal but lossy (32 % absorbed); with port 2 shorted Γin = 0.617∠43.7° and RL = 4.19 dB; after the 45° shift S₁₁′ = 0.2∠−90° and S₂₁′ = 0.8∠−105°.

traps: Treating |S₂₁| as a dB value. A magnitude of 0.9 is −0.92 dB; convert with 20 log₁₀|S₂₁|.
Using S₁₁ as the input reflection when port 2 is not matched. With a load Γ<sub>L</sub> ≠ 0, use Γin = S₁₁ + S₁₂S₂₁Γ<sub>L</sub>/(1 − S₂₂Γ<sub>L</sub>).
Shifting every S-parameter by the same phase when a reference plane moves. Sₙₙ gets twice the line phase, an off-diagonal term once, and terms not touching port n none.
Calling a matrix lossless because its diagonal is zero. Matched and lossless are different tests: check the column sums |S₁ⱼ|² + |S₂ⱼ|² + … = 1.
Swapping S₁₂ and S₂₁. The first index is the port the wave leaves, the second the port it enters: S₂₁ is from 1 to 2.

quiz.a: S₂₁ = b₂/a₁ with a₂ = 0, that is, with port 2 ended in a matched load. It is the forward transmission coefficient from port 1 to port 2.

quiz.q: Why are S-parameters preferred to Z- or Y-parameters at microwave frequencies?
quiz.a: Z and Y need open or short terminations. At microwave frequencies an open end radiates, a short has inductance and an active device may oscillate. S-parameters need only matched loads, which are easy to make, and they relate directly to power through |Sᵢⱼ|².

quiz.q: A two-port has |S₁₁| = 0.1 and |S₂₁| = 0.5. Find the return loss, input VSWR and insertion loss.
quiz.a: RL = −20 log₁₀(0.1) = 20 dB. VSWR = 1.1/0.9 = 1.22. IL = −20 log₁₀(0.5) = 6.02 dB. Since 0.01 + 0.25 = 0.26 < 1, the device absorbs 74 % of the power: it is lossy.

quiz.q: A matched attenuator has |S₂₁| = 0.316. Find its insertion loss.
quiz.a: IL = −20 log₁₀(0.316) = 10.0 dB: one tenth of the power gets through.

quiz.q: A reciprocal two-port has S₁₁ = S₂₂ = 0 and |S₂₁| = 1. Show that it is lossless.
quiz.a: Reciprocal gives S₁₂ = S₂₁. Column 1: |S₁₁|² + |S₂₁|² = 0 + 1 = 1; column 2: |S₁₂|² + |S₂₂|² = 1. Columns 1 and 2 are orthogonal: S₁₁S*₁₂ + S₂₁S*₂₂ = 0 + 0 = 0. So S†S = I: it is a matched lossless line section.

quiz.q: An isolator has S₂₁ = 0.95 and S₁₂ = 0.03 with both ports matched. Is it reciprocal? Is it lossless?
quiz.a: Not reciprocal, since S₁₂ ≠ S₂₁. Not lossless: column 2 gives |S₁₂|² + |S₂₂|² = 0.0009, far below 1, so almost all the reverse power is absorbed. That absorption is the job of an isolator.

quiz.q: The port-2 reference plane of a device is moved outward by βl = 30°. How do S₁₁, S₂₁ and S₂₂ change?
quiz.a: S₁₁ does not touch port 2, so it is unchanged. S₂₁ gets e<sup>−j30°</sup> (30° more lag). S₂₂ crosses the extra line twice and gets e<sup>−j60°</sup>. No magnitude changes.

beyond: S-parameters are stored in Touchstone files (.s2p for a two-port), which circuit simulators read directly. High-speed digital design uses mixed-mode S-parameters for differential pairs, and de-embedding removes test fixtures from a measurement. Search for "Touchstone file format", "mixed-mode S-parameters" and "de-embedding".
